subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PLANS FOR FUTURE PROGRAMS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The matter of urgent and pressing necessity arises from the revelation today that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) plans a drastic change in the government's multicultural program, which follows upon the elimination, following the 1974 general election, of a minister who was exclusively responsible for multicultural programs in the country.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow):
That this House reject the program proposed by the Minister of Labour as reported in today's press and urge the minister to make a statement at the earliest possible time on the government's future plans for multicultural programming.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important and urgent issue.
Since within the framework of our present judicial system the policemen are the first to carry the can as the result of paroles among which are noted many relapses and offences of all kinds and considering that we must protect those who maintain order and protect honest citizens and that they must have a say in the matter of parole, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That the House should consider the matter immediately to enable the federal government to set up a committee responsible for paroles, whose membership would include in addition to the usual members, the police director of each provincial police force as well as representatives
of the municipal and federal police forces, so that they may take part in the decisions to that effect.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to, I suspect, the only friend of the farmers and marketing boards in the whole cabinet, the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the government's policy that farmers and fishermen are exempt from the guidelines under the anti-inflation program, and in view of the fact that a government document says that these boards will have to be reviewed before reaching firm decisions on which ones should be subject to the guidelines and which of their costs should be allowable, may I ask the Minister of Agriculture whether he can tell the House if it is still the position of the government that they are exempt from the guidelines; can the minister explain how that statement is compatible with the willingness of the AntiInflation Board to make scapegoats of the marketing boards, ignoring wholesalers, processors and packagers; and does the minister intend to see that the farmers and fishermen remain exempt under the guidelines?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me say again that some editorial writers have been grossly inaccurate about how marketing boards operate. They are under strict guidelines, just as strict as the guidelines that are going to apply to industry and labour.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MINISTERIAL PERMITS
speechtext:
1. The 1971 Census of Canada was a self-enumeration Census and the following language questions were asked: 1. Mother tongue-Language first spoken and still understood: English, French, German, Italian, Other. 2. What language do you most often speak at home now? English, French, German, Indian, Italian, Magyar, Netherlands, Polish, Ukrainian, Yiddish, Other. 3. Can you speak English or French well enough to conduct a conversation? English only, French only, Both English and French, Neither English nor French. In the processing of the 1971 Census data a series of procedures was implemented to eliminate all the inconsistencies in the data being produced. The editing instruction referred to was one of these procedures. It ensured that if a respondent reported one of the official languages as mother tongue and the other official language as language most often spoken at home, then the response to the third question (Can you speak English or French well enough to conduct a conversation?), was changed to both English and French. This editing procedure produced the following results: 97,500 persons who originally reported English only for the third question changed to both English and French. 32,400 persons who originally reported French only to the third question were changed to both English and French. 2,450 persons who originally reported neither English nor French to the third question were changed to both English and French. In total 132,350 persons or 4.6 per cent of the bilingual population were added to the population claiming ability to carry on a conversation in both English and French. In addition, if the responses to the question on mother tongue, and to the question on language most often spoken at home were both English, or both French, and the response to the third question was neither English nor French, the following ensued: 113,480 persons reporting neither English nor French to the third question were changed to English only. This was 0.8 per cent of the English only population. 36,130 persons reporting neither English nor French to the third question were changed to French only. This was 0.9 per cent of the French only population. There was no inflation of the number of French speaking only citizens due to these procedures. Editing procedures were finalized on January 11, 1971 and all processing and publication of data have taken these edits into account. The data given above are available at the national level only.

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code

The House resumed from Friday, November 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-61, to provide a maritime code for Canada, to amend the Canada Shipping Act and other acts in consequence thereof and to enact other consequential or related provisions, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a long, deep and abiding commitment to this issue because of my background in Vancouver, my service during the war in Coastal Command in the air force, my living abroad representing Canada, not to mention, of course, my having been born in Saskatchewan. I am sorry that the other members of the Saskatchewan contingent are not here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: They are here.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
From my present residence I look out over one of the great shipping lanes of the world. I deny there is a conflict of interest here. I would suggest instead there is a confluence of interests - everything comes together from my background to give me an interest, a real true interest in the Darling report.
We have waited at least five years for this legislation. The Darling report was issued in October, 1970, and here we are in November, 1975, five long years later. For years many of us have been advocating what this legislation imperfectly proposes - basically reserving the coastal trade for Canadian vessels and a code covering certain aspects of maritime matters.
Our delight at getting a final look at positive legislation therefore is tempered as soon as we read the bill, by a growing realization that the provisions are no more than a partial answer to our long felt needs - the long felt needs of Canada.
I suggest, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that this is no more than a promise that "there will be ships on the slips by and by". Unfortunately, we are now dealing with only one of the matters related to our merchant marine.
Let us start by looking at some of the recommendations in the Darling report to see how they are matched in the legislation. I suggest that recommendations Nos. 2, 3, 4, 10, 12, 13 and 15 are dealt with in one way or another in the legislation.
No. 1 deals with the coasting trade; No. 2 with the coasting trade extended to something beyond the normal commercial operation; No. 3 with the continental shelf and territorial seas, bringing us up to date in terms of marine multilateral negotiations; No. 4 with a very dangerous area and one we have been putting up with long enough and one that I thought we were going to get rid of, that is, issuing permits to non-Canadian flag bearers - I shall be returning to this; No. 10 is related in many respects to No. 2, exploitation and exploration around our shores; No. 12 to

government operated marine insurance which unfortunately we do not see much of in this bill, and No. 13 dealing with steamship inspection which I understand we are promised in another edition of this bill.
Judging from the performance of the government in fulfilling its promises, I wonder if we are going to have to wait another five years for two more "books" as they are being called. I hope I am wrong in my suspicions, but I will continue to hold them until I am proved wrong.
Recommendation No. 15 in the Darling report relates to the Alaska Panhandle and is of particular interest. That is not being dealt with in the legislation, and I would hope the parliamentary secretary would be able to nudge the other member of the Saskatchewan triumvirate dealing with the merchant marine in order to let us know whether there are any conversations going on relating to this recommendation, in which it is suggested that Canada should have some special privileges of access through the Alaska Panhandle.
I mentioned that I am distressed the minister is not here but I hope the parliamentary secretary will take note of the matters that are going to be raised, because we have very real concerns. There are gaps in this legislation that we want to draw to the attention of the government. But we are not going to delay the bill unduly because we think it should get to committee where we will be able to explore matters more fully.
Time will permit me to deal with only one or two important matters raised in the legislation, or excluded from it. I shall concern myself with the matters of crewing, and cabotage. The code, included as a schedule at the end of the bill, cannot be considered as complete. I wonder of what use an incomplete maritime code can be? What is such a code if it is not complete and does not deal with certain important matters?
Conspicuous by their absence are provisions dealing with inspection services, standards of shipbuilding, requirements for icebreaking in various areas, and requirements for crewing. If my memory serves me right, the parliamentary secretary suggested that bills we can expect later will deal with crewing and shipbuilding standards. I wonder if these will come under new paragraph Bill-74, or under some completely different code. Frankly I think a maritime code should be just that: There should be just one maritime code, not several, for the sake of simplicity, so that it is available to masters and shore workers, who may know exactly what is involved.
It has been suggested on a number of occasions that we should not be talking of a Canadian merchant marine because of past difficulties we experienced. When a Canadian merchant service existed there was a good deal of trouble with crewing. I draw to the attention of the House that the major crewing union which would be involved with the merchant service has undertaken not to engage in strike action for ten years. According to The Canadian Sailor of July 28, 1975:
The Seafarers International Union (SIU) is willing to sign a 10 year, no-strike agreement with Canadian flag operators for ships in high seas service.
November 26, 1975

It follows, I think, that the union will extend the ten year no-strike agreement to operators of Canadian flag ships sailing in coastal waters. This brings me to my next point.
Not long ago the attorney of the SIU sent the former minister of transport a letter protesting against the appearance in our coastal trade of a ship bearing a name well known in Russian literature, Alexandr Puskin, which planned to operate summer cruises wholly within the territorial limits of Canada. Departures were scheduled from Montreal on August 10 and 17. And they happened.
This, of course, raises the problem of cabotage. I looked for the meaning of cabotage in the dictionary on the Table, but found that the origin is unknown. I then consulted another dictionary in the library, and found that cabotage is derived from the old French term "cabo", which comes from the Spanish cabo meaning cape. If we go back, we find that it means from cape to cape along the shore line; hence, cabotage. That is how sailors sailed in days of old, from cape to cape. That is the meaning of cabotage. But cabotage has come to mean more than this. It applies to the transport of passengers and freight by sea and air. The rule in the air is rigorously defended.
A foreign air carrier cannot embark a passenger in Toronto and drop him in Winnipeg. That privilege is open to the Canadian flag carrier only. That is cabotage. The foreign air carrier can pick up a passenger in a foreign country and drop him in Winnipeg or Toronto, but cannot carry a passenger between two Canadian points. The principle of cabotage is involved.
I say that our rights to our own maritime cabotage are being invaded by foreign flag vessels. Ministerial permits may be granted to foreign flag carriers who wish to indulge in this trade. I say we ought to encourage the construction of Canadian vessels, and let them engage in the cabotage business. They alone should carry freight and passengers in our waters.
Some foreign flag vessels try to circumvent the problem by calling, during their travels in our waters, at nonCanadian ports. Let us say, if they try to respect the principles of cabotage, that they go from Montreal to St. Pierre and Miquelon, down the south shore, then back to St. Pierre and Miquelon, and then to another Canadian port. They can claim that they interrupted their journey by calling at non-Canadian ports. This is how it is being done.
Let me put on record the route the Alexandr Puskin followed last summer. The ship engaged in cabotage within our waters. The route was: Montreal, Quebec, Bagotville, Perce, St. Pierre and Miquelon (weather permitting), and back to Montreal. The Alexandr Puskin was not the only ship to operate in our waters last summer. The Danish vessel M/V Discoverer did the same on our Great Lakes. Its route was: Montreal, Toronto, Welland, Windsor, Parry Sound, Mackinac, Chicago, and back. This is an affront, a denial of cabotage which ought to belong to the coastal state.
This particular legislation does not deal with cabotage, in the sense of reserving such rights for Canadian flag vessels, and therein lies one of the great defects of the bill.
Clause 8(3) defines our coasting trade. It says:
. . . 'coasting trade of Canada' includes
Maritime Code
(a)	the carriage of goods by water or by land and water, the carriage
of passengers by water land towage,
(i) from one port or place in Canada to the same or another port or place in Canada.
That is a perfectly good definition. On the other hand, clause 8 subclause (5) reads:
Where the Governor in Council by order issued under the authority of this subsection, so declares, the coasting trade of Canada does not, during such period of time as is specified in the order, include such of the following as are specified in the order,
(a)	the carriage by water of goods or of such classes of goods as are
specified in the order,
(b)	the carriage by water of passengers, and
(c)	towage ...
Therefor we know what the coasting trade is, and is not. Clause 11 really puts the cap on it. It says:
(1) Upon application made to it by a person resident in Canada who wishes to utilize the services of a particular ship, other than a Canadian ship, in the coasting trade of Canada, the Canadian Transport Commission may issue a licence ...
I take it that the "person" referred to means a legal person or entity. Under the provisions of clause 11 the issuance of a licence is to be related to "the public interest". The question is, who will define "the public interest"? Obviously it is in the interest of the operator of a foreign flag vessel who wishes to capture our cabotage trade to urge that it is in Canada's public interest for him to be allowed to do so. Where is there encouragement for Canadian flag vessels to operate in this fashion? The Stella Maris, under Greek flag, also operated in the Great Lakes last summer.
We encounter the same difficulty on the west coast. We have only one Canadian flag vessel on the west coast. We have a Norwegian flag vessel The Royal Viking on the west coast doing the Victoria, Juneau, Skagway, Sitka, Prince Rupert and Vancouver route. The Prinzendam, under the Dutch flag and with an Indonesian crew, is doing Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Tracey-Arm, Juneau, Skagway, Glacier Bay, Ketchikan, Alert Bay and Vancouver. The only vessel that is of Canadian registry is the Princess Patricia which does this same route. Surely there is some way of dealing with this problem. It has to be tightened up. I am afraid that clause 8, subclause (5) and clause (11) do not deal with it very satisfactorily. Surely the public interest as mentioned in clause (11) is that these cruise passengers in particular be carried on Canadian ships, built in Canada and crewed by Canadian crews! That is "the public interest" in any law that I want to have anything to do with here.
It has often been said, and it has been said to me privately and in letters I have received from some of my constituents, that it would be too costly to build and man our own ships. However, what are the real costs in Canadian terms? I quote very reliable figures. Last year Canada spent $2.7 billion, paying it to foreign shippers, in shipping charges for all categories of Canada's exports and imports. That is the real cost in Canadian terms, $2.7 billion. These funds should have remained in Canada. They should have been paid to Canadian carriers to carry our goods abroad and to bring to this country at least some of the goods we want to consume.

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code
I am not alone in advocating this form of activity for Canada which, after all, is part of Canada's tradition. Not only can I lay claim to having been born in Saskatchewan, but I can trace my origin through my mother to Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Even better.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
I have great faith in the breadth of this dominion from coast to coast. In Nova Scotia we used to build some of the great traders of the world for the tea trade and the grain trade. Great racers were built in Nova Scotian yards. We built great ships on the west coast as well.
I suggest that the minister get in touch with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson). On February 25 of this year the National Council of the Navy League of Canada submitted a brief to the Minister of National Defence in which they made a great point of this matter. I quote from the submission:
Recent developments are dictating a change in this attitude (towards Canadian registered shipping) because of our extensive offshore continental shelf areas, rich in mineral, oil and fishery resource potential, areas totalling a third the size of the land mass. With the depletion of the land based resources throughout the world these offshore resources become not only more valuable to Canada but increasingly more attractive to other nations and multi-national corporations. We must be alert to the fact that conflicts in the future, as in the past, will tend to generate around the needs for, and control of, essential resources; food and raw materials for industry.
It is the Navy League's contention that the value and importance of this offshore resource wealth has not been adequately recognized by the Canadian public or the government. The interests are fragmented and dispersed through a number of organizations ...
No longer simply a capability to defend one's country from attack from across the oceans, seapower is now recognized as the capability to use the oceans in any way required to further the national aims of the country, through military, economic or political strength. It calls for strong, effective maritime forces; a modern, efficient merchant marine not subject to foreign control; a healthy fishing industry,-"
That is a submission made to the government. I do not know whether a copy went to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). If not, I have at least had an opportunity to draw it to his attention.
We can only regret that there has been such a long delay in bringing forth this measure. Our merchant marine has virtually disappeared through a lack of nutrients. I would like once again to put something on record. I find in this House that unfortunately you have to put on the record every four or five months facts which somehow or other come to be neglected.
In 1948 Canada had 203 dry cargo merchant vessels of
10,000	tons or more. In 1958 this was down to five and some of them, I can assure you, were nowhere near 10,000 tons. In the period 1968 to 1972, when this government was in power, we lost even those three. We lost the fleet we had in 1968. All that remains are three vessels of the 5,000 ton class.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
We lost more than that in 1968.
An hon. Member; Yes, you lost the election.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
As my colleague says, we lost a great deal in 1968. We hope that all is not lost,

especially now that the 200 mile-continental shelf concept is coming more and more to the fore in our thinking. It is most important that we act now in this area, with the widening area over which we expect to exercise jurisdiction, not just in fishing terms, but in terms of our trading practices.
As a major trading nation, a position we hold even if we were rejected as a participant in the Rambouillet conference, we need our own merchant fleet. Here is a strange thing. Your Honour will be interested to hear this as well as the members of this House. We Canadians are offering Algeria technical assistance through CIDA to create a merchant marine. That is what CIDA is up to. It has the gall, I guess that is the right word-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Temerity.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
-the temerity to offer technical assistance in the construction of a merchant marine to Algeria. When I first heard that I just did not believe it. I wanted to visit this school of merchant marine which was half way down the coast between Algiers and the Moroccan border, but unfortunately I did not have the time to get there. We seem to pretend that we know something about the merchant marine. However, it has to be said that this government that has decided to help the Algerians does not want to help Canadians.
As to our ability to design and build our own ships, I have already referred to the shipbuilding tradition on both coasts. I have not mentioned the need of protecting and ensuring our sovereignty in the Arctic which shipbuilders on both coasts are prepared, ready, and able to do. I suggest that we have a great number of imaginative ship designers. One of the companies in my constituency has been working for some time to have organized at the University of British Columbia a school of naval architecture and marine engineering. They have been working on this for two or three years because of the belief that technology in this area, as in all others, cannot be bought economically. It has to be developed at home to prove really worthwhile. If you import, you are going to pay through the nose for it. We do have the native genius here. I mentioned the other night something we have in the way of car design. But we also have native genius in ship design also just by virtue of the fact that we are a maritime nation with extended coast lines. This project to create at the University of British Columbia a school of naval architecture lacks some $50,000 to get it going.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Get it from the Algerians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
We might go to the Algerians. They, after all, as I understand it, are one of the OPEC nations. I will collect a few members of the House and perhaps we will set off as a delegation at Easter time, or at Christmas time, and see if we can raise this $50,000 from the Algerians for this school of naval architecture in British Columbia.
To those who doubt the imaginative ability of our shipbuilding firms I suggest that the next time they are in the library they should take a look at a copy of Canadian Shipping and Marine Engineering, which I receive regular-
November 26, 1975

ly. I enjoy looking through it. There are some extraordinarily imaginative designs for ships and maritime structures to be found in its pages. One of the designs which was prepared recently brought a ferry called the Chi-Cheemaun into being. My hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) may well have been aboard this particular ferry vessel. It was designed in my riding and built in Georgian Bay, I believe in his riding. Chi-Cheemaun, is the Ojibway word for "big canoe". In its modern form it is a ferry incorporating advanced first class technology and imaginative design. I am delighted that the opportunity should occur to pay tribute to the firm concerned.
There are many other things to be said about navigation and tanker routes. Time will not permit me to go much further or I might deal with the new products which are necessary to clean up polluted waters and preserve our maritime heritage.
Much has yet to be said about other aspects of the bill, for example about the centralization of the registry and the difficulty this is likely to cause to those living in the outports. One of my hon. friends may be addressing himself to that aspect. However, having talked principally about cabotage, which really offends me as a Canadian, my suggestion is that we terminate our comments quickly and get the bill to committee where hon. members can call witnesses and examine it in detail. We certainly do not plan to hold it up.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) would mind repeating his remarks regarding Alert Bay.' I heard the name mentioned but I did not get the import of his comments.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: I would be happy to oblige the hon. member. The vessel to which I referred was the Prinzendam, a Dutch registered vessel of the Holland-America line, with an Indonesian crew. It carried out a couple of cruises last summer from Vancouver to Prince Rupert, Tracey Arm, Juneau, Skagway, Glacier Bay, Ketchikan, Alert Bay and Vancouver on the way back. It was simply cabotage. You can see that from Ketchikan to Alert Bay is one thing. That is not cabotage in the sense we have been talking about because that is from a foreign port to a Canadian port, but if they picked up passengers in Alert Bay to deliver them in Vancouver they were engaging in cabotage, an enterprise which, as defined in this bill, should be carried out by a Canadian flag carrier.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) for the information he has given me, Mr. Speaker. Alert Bay harbour has been used quite extensively by ships plying between California and Alaska. They drop anchor in Alert Bay since there is a large community of native people there. It has become quite a tourist attraction for American ships travelling along the coast line. The practice also supplies much needed revenue to that community.
I do not wish to take up very much time this afternoon, but I do wish to say I favour the replacement of the myriads of directions which the Maritime Code is intended to supplant. The proposal to incorporate some of the
Maritime Code
recommendations of the Darling Report is, I believe, progressive. The provisions defining Canadian ships and relating to the plying of Canadian waters by Canadian ships except where special licences have been granted, constitute a step in the right direction. I hope, however, that we do not get into the situation in which the United States found itself some time ago following the requirement that ships plying between United States ports must carry United States cargo.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: The other way round.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: In other words, lumber, for example, sent from one coast to the other has to be carried in American ships, which is very expensive. I hope we do not get into that kind of situation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: What's wrong with that?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
The cost of shipping in the U.S. is one reason why we are able to compete with American lumber on American markets. It is because we are able to ship more cheaply than they are.
I should like to discuss clause 15 on page 56 where the following item is to be found, numbered Bll-15:
Every ship that exceeds 10 metres in length and is owned by a person or persons each of whom is qualified to own a Canadian registered ship shall be registered in accordance with this code.
The succeeding provision covers vessels which do not exceed 10 metres in length and provides for their registration as small craft.
I thought that perhaps some of the hon. members from the east coast, or possibly some members of the opposition parties who come from the west coast would object very strongly to the proposition put forward in clause 24 on page 59 which states:
A central office for the filing of documents relating to ships owned by persons qualified to own Canadian ships shall be established in the national capital region described in the schedule to the National Capital Act.
I am not sure what will be the reaction to that provision of hon. members who come from the east coast or the west coast, but I would point out that already we have in Vancouver, Victoria, and Prince Rupert three registry offices and, honestly, I do not see the necessity of shutting down those three local regional offices and replacing them by one office in Ottawa. It is rather like deciding that all British Columbia motor vehicles should be registered in Ottawa. If hon. members would check the registry in British Columbia, for example, they would find out that the number of craft registered there exceeds several thousand.
It appears it would be necessary under this proposal to send the relevant information to Ottawa by telegraph or mail, or some other means, where presumably it will be available for use at points which are some 3,000 miles away. If someone could explain to me how this would create a better system than the regional system we already have, I would appreciate it. I have seen many situations of a similar nature where regional matters have been shifted to Ottawa when they could have been handled very well locally, and I think this is a perfect example.

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code
I thank the House for having had the opportunity of putting this matter in front of the House prior to this bill going to committee and becoming law. I honestly think that if at some time in the future a central registry is established we will have to consider legislation to turn matters over once again to regional offices. I am sure that the three regional offices in British Columbia are much more capable of handling registrations for the province of British Columbia than Ottawa.
I trust I shall have the support in committee of members of the opposition in either amending or deleting this particular section of the bill. It is not the most important section, but it is a necessity that the regional area offices are kept open. Surely it should not be a case of meeting the convenience of the government. We are not living in a state that does things only for the convenience of government; I hope we are living in a country where things are done for the convenience of citizens. With that, Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members of the opposition for their support and I trust we will be able either to amend or delete the section to which I have referred.

speechtext: The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: We will now hear from a good inland sailor.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, members from the east and west coasts sometimes forget that Ontario has a salt water coast as well.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
So has
Manitoba.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
The use we have made of this salt water coast has been indicative of the interest other members from the maritimes have shown toward the utilization of that coast. Now that they have come to appreciate some advantages in their own areas they may be more willing to give some assistance to Manitoba and Ontario which share a common salt water coast.
Coming from an inland area I should like to say I am pleased to support this legislation. We have been developing our sea coast for some 20 or 25 years, and I hope we are now in for a number of changes, this legislation being one of the first and necessary steps that have to be taken.
During the war, and in the period leading up to the war, Canada had a large number of vessels in service for interport trade. It also had Liberty ships, as well as a number of other ships of a similar nature engaged in international service and flying the Canadian flag. As a matter of fact Canada was starting to give credence to the desire to be a third power nation, a nation aware of its trading destiny and of the necessity for a merchant fleet to handle its trade.
Canada has the largest, or certainly one of the largest coast lines in the world. We also are one of the biggest trading nations. We import and export about $15 billion worth of trade a year. To the best of my knowledge there are only three ships of Canadian registry sailing in international waters. For a country with the longest coast line
[Mr. Anderson.)
in the world and with one of the largest trading patterns in the world to have three miserable ships flying the Canadian flag must be a disgrace even to this government.
Only recently has it become possible for us to look at this situation in an impassionate way. It was C. D. Howe who, in large degree, was responsible for building up the Canadian Liberty ship fleet. It was also necessary for financial reasons to get rid of that fleet. He was well aware that all through the history of merchant navies they had to be subsidized, from the Phoenicians, the Egyptians, the Romans on. Since these fleets reflected the image of these people to others, they also became part of their development. In the same way, Mr. Speaker, these ships were subsidized when they were needed during the war. However, after the war we were not willing to continue the subsidies so our shipping fleet was dispersed.
Interest in the development of a Canadian merchant marine has been highlighted by an organization that has received a lot of comment in this House, most of it unfavourable. However, these comments were seldom backed up and there has been much hysteria about this organization. I am referring to the SIU. Some years ago a member of the House who was then the member for a riding in Montreal, the honourable member for Skeena, and myself were asked to attend a conference on safety on the Great Lakes. Since that time the Montreal member become a member of the cabinet, and he is now the member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner). At that time, however, he was parliamentary secretary to the minister of transport, and he invited the then honourable member for Skeena and I to go with him to this conference.
The conference was called by the SIU and was attended by marine workers, the pilots association, a number of employee agencies, as well as all shipping companies operating on the Great Lakes. Safety conditions on the lakes were so bad that these bodies got together and agreed at the meeting to establish a ship-to-shore radio safety protection system. But who opposed that, Mr. Speaker? The Department of Transport. Shortly after the parliamentary secretary of that day came back to Ottawa, the deputy minister of transport was moved to another portfolio. That has been my experience of civil servants attached to the Department of Transport, and it has also been my experience that most government members were not really interested in taking action to deal with shipping problems; they merely discussed them.
Over the years representatives of the SIU came to Ottawa on a regular basis. They talked of the Darling report and of the need to control coastal trade in Canada, of having Canadian goods carried in Canadian bottoms that flew the Canadian flag and were manned by Canadian crews. They were very interested in this for a very selfish reason, if for none other. If these were Canadian crews operating under the Canadian flag, they would be able to organize them.
I think there was a much greater interest than that which involves something we really have not thought about very much. If we are to have a coastal trade we must build ships somewhere, and we are not building ships at this time.
November 26, 1975

These people were joined on a number of occasions by other organizations which wanted to implement the Darling report. They came to us regularly. Finally, Leonard McLaughlin, who was the president of the SIU, established an office in Ottawa. He was one of the few people that openly lobbied the government strongly on the basis of building more Canadian ships, and having more Canadian seamen operating our ships under the Canadian flag.
I am surprised to learn that the Canadian Pacific operates under the Liberian flag, the Panamanian flag, or the flag of some other country. It does not operate under the Canadian flag.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Not passenger
vessels.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: How many passenger boats do they have? They have a few ferries kicking around and one or two passenger ships, but they operate a lot of ships and not under the Canadian flag. The Canadian National Railways operates ships through subsidiary organizations in this country, but not under the Canadian flag, and this is really the Canadian government which does not in fact support the idea of having our own Canadian merchant navy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Merchant marine.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: There has not been much support in this regard from the government. There has been some incidental and continuous support, sometimes vigorous, from some members of this House, but we as representatives of the Canadian public generally have not really been in favour of the idea of establishing a merchant navy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: Speak for yourself.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: There have been some people dedicated to this and I would include among them Leonard McLaughlin, a former president of the SIU, and Mr. Gralewicz, the president at the present time. They have carried on this type of lobby for the development of a Canadian merchant navy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: A Canadian merchant marine.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Coming from inland waters I mix up navy with marine, but it seems to me they are the same thing. I suppose there is a difference. This reminds me of an occasion when I negotiated a contract for a plywood company. I kept talking about veneer and they kept talking about plywood. They were always upset when I talked about veneer, and it took me some time to find out that veneer was not necessarily plywood, but plywood was always veneer. I learned it the hard way, and I hope perhaps I will learn something about this idea of a Canadian merchant navy.
In this bill we are providing a grandfather clause to the Commonwealth agreement for a period of five years. We will not be able to move into Canadian registry unless we have some ships, and we had better start building those ships right now. If we do not I can foresee what the government will do. It will offer permits to anybody anywhere who has got a ship to come into our waters, and it will not demand any money for the permits. It will not
Maritime Code
demand that Canadian crews man those ships, and it will not demand that the Canadian flag be flown. The Government will not demand that our labour standards be upheld on those ships.
These ships will still be operating under the Liberian or Panamanian flags, or any other runaway flags of the world, because then they can hire crews without paying the required wages, and if they kill somebody because of unsafe conditions they can just dump him overboard and nobody will ask any questions. We will still be operating under those conditions unless we implement another part of the Darling report which recommends that we establish a merchant shipbuilding facility.
As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) has mentioned, Canadians have done good design work. Canadians will always be remembered for their ability in respect of marine shipbuilding. We have done some excellent shipbuilding in Midland, as the member has suggested, and I am sure there are some ships being built on the west coast and on the east coast. Unfortunately it is not the Canadian government or the Canadian industry that is building them.
No matter how much members of this House may desire it, I suggest these ships will not be built or operated by private industry alone. This requires a combination of private industry and government. A considerable amount of money will have to be put into the shipbuilding industry by the government, and I suggest this would be worth while.
In concluding, let me say that we have not mentioned containerization or our inability to get into that field. We need private facilities operated under government auspices in order that we can provide a merchant marine with the shore facilities. I have not referred to northern services, but if we are not to lose our Arctic potential or, in fact, our sovereignty, we will have to put ships into that area.
Let us remember what has happened to our fishing fleets. We cannot protect them. We do not have enough ships for surveillance or to stop foreign fleets from fishing offshore without our consent. We are not able to supervise this because we do not have the ships. We will not be able to maintain our sovereignty in the north until we establish a shipbuilding industry that will provide the ships we need under the Canadian flag.
As a Canadian I certainly hope I will live long enough to see a Canadian merchant marine flying the Canadian flag, or whatever the flag is that ships fly at sea. It is a little different because it is a seagoing flag. I hope they will fly the flag that will carry across the world, along with our goods, the reputation of Canada as a trading and a seagoing nation. We have large coastal areas in Canada, and three ships will never provide the required merchant marine services of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the introduction of the Maritime Code, Bill C-61, which I believe was initially introduced on July 23, 1973, and on which the government has been stalling ever since. I welcome the bill because of my background and as a former ship owner in my native town of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia.
9478

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code
I can remember growing up in that area and watching the original Bluenose, the Haligonian and some 100 other deep-sea bankers, as we called our sailing schooners, as they raced out of Lunenburg Harbour to our continental shelf in search of the cod and other species which were utilized in the area. Later on I spent some time on my own ships, and I say to you, Sir, that anyone who has ever smelled the tar and oakum on the deck of a ship, or felt the ship creaking and rolling under his feet, will never quite forget that particular experience.
This bill is basically an overhaul of the regulations covering Canadian shipping, the first I believe since the 1930's. It is really the first overhaul since that time, because then we largely adopted the United Kingdom statute. This housekeeping bill is really not complete, and we on this side of the House are still awaiting the additional shipbuilding assistance legislation that has been promised us now for several years.
There are few members in the House who can speak with authority on this bill, a bill which contains a total of 84 pages and which covers not only the Canada Shipping Act but other acts as well. For this reason we on this side of the House want to be assured of the fullest participation and involvement of Canadian shipping interests when the bill goes to committee. Such groups as the Dominion Marine Association, the Canadian Shipbuilding Association, the Canadian ship repair group, as well as representatives of the unions concerned with shipbuilding should be invited to appear before the committee and give the members the benefit of their views and their knowledge on this particular subject.
As I said a moment ago, this bill is a rewrite of the Canada Shipping. Act, and in clauses 1 to 8 are the technical explanations. Clause 8 states:
(1)	Except in accordance with a permit issued pursuant to section 10 or a licence issued pursuant to section 11, no ship other than a Canadian ship shall engage in the coasting trade of Canada.
In other words, this section preserves the coasting trade for Canadian ships in accordance with the declaration of the former minister of transport on September 24, 1973. He gave the British Commonwealth Shipping Agreement one year's notice that he would give notice of withdrawal at a later date. In the spring of 1974 he finally gave that notice, so in the spring of 1975 we were finally on our own. The former act, as hon. members are aware, gave so-called Canadian recognition to any ship of any country in the British Commonwealth Shipping Agreement, such as Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, etc. So in this respect the legislation is finally being brought up to date.
Clause 8 goes on to state:
(2)	For the purposes of this section and sections 11, 12, and 14, a "Canadian ship" means
(a)	a ship built and registered in Canada, or
(b)	a foreign built Canadian registered ship upon which full custom duty has been paid.
The term "the coasting trade of Canada" includes:
(a)	the carriage of goods by water or by land and water, the carriage of passengers by water, and towage,
(i) from one port or place in Canada to the same or another port or place in Canada,
(Mr. Crouse.]
(ii) between a port or place in Canada and any marine structure that is engaged in exploration for or exploitation of natural resources in accordance with a permit or licence issued pursuant to an act of parliament or of the legislature of a province,
This clause appears to me to protect the trade which may exist for Canadians between the mainland and any offshore drilling rigs operating off our coast on our continental shelf. Unfortunately, however, the conflict of jurisdiction over these resources between the provincial and the federal governments, as well as the conflict in the grey area called Georges Bank between the government of the United States, the governments of Maine and Massachusetts, and the Canadian government, have seriously cooled the initiative previously shown by the major oil companies in developing any resources of oil or gas which may exist in this area.
When we learn, as we did recently, that our supplies of oil and gas are drying up and that shipments to the United States must be curtailed by one third, it seems to me that the government should takes steps immediately to resolve the ownership problem on offshore resources. Every effort should be made to determine the proper authority which should receive royalty payments from oil and gas discoveries. The heads of the oil companies have stated publicly that they are willing to pay royalties to someone, but they are not willing to become involved in a legislative hassle between the provincial governments in Atlantic Canada and the federal government in Ottawa, or in a dispute between Washington and Ottawa over ownership of offshore resources.
In my opinion this dispute must be resolved quickly, or otherwise subclause 8(2)(a) and clause 9 are meaningless for we will have no marine structures engaged in the resource development off our coast which will require the services of a Canadian ship. It is as simple as that. We believe from tests made that there are resources there, but the oil companies are mute and have withdrawn their oil drilling rigs from the area. They are obviously waiting for a sign, and the onus is on the government to provide that sign of encouragement which means we will proceed to examine, study, and develop any possible resource we may have in that area.
Clause 10 deals with those whom we exempt. It reads:
1. Upon application made to it by the owner of a ship, the Canadian Transport Commission may issue, without charge, a permit authorizing the ship to engage in the coasting trade of Canada for a period specified in the permit not exceeding twelve months from the day on which the permit is issued.
However, no permit shall be issued unless the applicant establishes to the satisfaction of the commission that on September 24, 1973, and at all times between that date and the day on which the application was filed, the ship to which the application relates was registered in a Commonwealth country, and in the twelve month period immediately preceding September 24, 1973, the ship was lawfully engaged in the coasting trade of Canada. However, there shall be no permit renewals for a date later than April 26, 1980.
Currently we exempt hundreds of ships a year from the provisions of the present act. We had been dishing out exemptions at a greater rate since this spring. However, the former minister of transport said in 1973 that there would be a five year-phase-in period, and in this period
November 26, 1975

so-called grandfather rights would be recognized. In my opinion this pledge should have been accepted when this legislation was drawn up, and in the period between now and 1978 the government should have laid down the guidelines which would lead to the construction of sufficient Canadian ships to look after the requirements of Canadian industry.
According to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) last year Canada spent $2.7 billion on shipping charges for all categories of exports and imports. More than $1.5 billion of that amount is reliably estimated to have been directed to the agents and operators of foreign ocean shipping lines which serve our ocean shipping needs. Unfortunately-and I say this with deep sincerity-the vast bulk of this trade is carried in ships owned, operated, crewed by and paying taxes to and earning profits for non-Canadian entrepreneurs and foreign national governments. More to the point, there is no lasting employment, investment or increased manufacturing activity flowing to Canada from this vast expenditure of our currency. It is surely worth while considering the scale of the operation to examine why Canadian firms and Canadian ships do not participate in this trade.
I believe it is necessary for us to look at the arguments for as well as those against the establishment of a Canadian flag fleet capable of participating in the international seaborn trade. There are many arguments which can be put forward on behalf of establishing a Canadian merchant marine. After all, a ship is like a small city. As I said at the beginning of my speech, I grew up in an area where shipbuilding is of primary importance. A ship requires heat, light, and water, and the installation of these facilities alone provides employment to many different trades.
Ship construction provides jobs in the shipyards, and once completed a ship is constantly providing employment to the ship repair industries, to the crews employed to man her, plus taxes to provincial governments and to federal authorities for the supplies that are required to keep a ship operational. In fact, I know of few endeavours which would stimulate our economy in a manner comparable to shipbuilding.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: And it's pollution free.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
As my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), states, it is a stimulation to the economy which is pollution free.
We saw this happen in Atlantic Canada when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister of this country. At that time the Conservative administration of the day decided as a national policy to stimulate the shipbuilding industry by the payment of subsidies on fishing trawlers.
The shipyards are still there in Atlantic Canada, still in central Canada, and still on the west coast of this country. All that is needed is a viable policy by the government which will encourage entrepreneurs and shipping minded individuals once again to invest in the construction of deep sea ships. If this action is not soon taken, we will lose the
Maritime Code
skills which we have to build ships, and then our later stage will be much worse than our present one.
Opponents of the Canadian flag fleet claim there is no requirement for a Canadian flag fleet. They state that all is well, and that we have no need to be apprehensive. Needless to say, those who most vigorously oppose such a fleet are the agents in Canada of those very foreign fleets now serving us. Being business minded they quite naturally look with a jaundiced eye upon the prospect of competition from any quarter. However, apart from the facts of commerce, everyone involved in the shipbuilding community knows that in creating a Canadian fleet not a job would be lost. I say that a considerable number would be gained, a fact of vital importance to this nation today, which has something like 8 per cent of its work force unemployed.
In his report tabled on October 19, 1970, entitled "The Elements of an International Shipping Policy for Canada", Howard Darling paints a gloomy picture of the situation facing the nation. He outlines the increasingly nationalistic character of the world fleets, upon which we depend almost entirely. He describes the increasing participation in and direction of these fleets by foreign governments.
Every major shipping nation in the world today is subsidizing its merchant shipping, and they are all insisting on the right to use subsidized fleets as an arm of their foreign policy. Darling's message is that the increasing capital cost of shipbuilding has driven ownership into fewer and fewer hands, hands which are increasingly controlled by foreign governments, and which are therefore no longer to be trusted with the reliable shipment of the $15 billion worth of goods which Canada annually imports and exports. I might add that these exports are vitally necessary if our economy is to survive. For example, Canada relies totally for the over water trans-shipment of manufactured goods and for the importation of oil from Arab and Venezuelan interests on these uncontrollable and fickle foreign carriers. We must ask ourselves what happens if there is a sustained shipping crisis and these carriers fail to show up.
I believe Canada must get on with the job of creating a national flag fleet while there is still time, before we are stranded without a fleet to carry our goods for international distribution. When we were faced with a real crisis at the beginning of the second world war the nation went ahead and established a fleet which was the envy of the world. We took people from Atlantic Canada, who naturally had salt water in their veins, and mixed them up with people from Saskatchewan and from the central provinces of this country, some of whom had never seen salt water, and we made sailors of the lot. They too established records, and were rewarded for their heroism by the amount of tonnage they carried to Great Britain in the cause of the allies during the second world war.
We can still do that today, but we must get on with the job. The changing situation is best illustrated by the recent United Nations trade and development committee proposal for a code of conduct for liner conferences. The self-proclaimed experts within the government point out that only a few countries have formally ratified this proposal. They conveniently ignore the fact that the proposal was supported by West Germany, Liberia, France, Panama, Russia, China, Japan, and 56 other nations with 55 per cent of the world's total general cargo shipping tonnage. Even if that
2995 6-48%

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code
specific United Nations proposal is not adopted, the message it contains is quite clear: developing nations want their goods carried in their own bottoms and are prepared to pay the price to rid themselves of their dependence upon foreign fleets. This is the point we must start considering in Canada, a most vitally important point.
Canada, typically, abstained at the United Nations, and today it is still unclear whether the government supports the UN resolution. The United Nations proposed that exporting or importing nations served by these liner conferences have the right to carry up to 40 per cent of their trade in their national vessels. Nationalism on the high seas was clearly asserted by that UN resolution.
To Canada, with 452 foreign registered ships serving in the liner conferences last year alone, the implications of the 40 per cent Canadian content would be a fleet of more than 175 ships.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext: That is what we want.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
And at some 40 men per ship the possibility exists for an additional 7,000 jobs at sea, not to mention staunching the flow of hard dollars from Canada to Athens, New York, and Tokyo. More important, our own fleet would guarantee us safe, reliable carriers under the direction of the Canadian government and operating under Canadian government policy.
What do we have at present? According to the latest figures available from the water committee of the Canadian Transport Commission, as of December 31, 1974, there were three dry cargo vessels registered in Canada engaged in the international seaborne trade. Two were constructed in 1961, while the third was built in 1958. Not one of these three ships was built in Canada. It is almost unbelievable, yet it is only too true.
Put in another way, not a single container ship, not a single tanker, not a single bulk carrier, and only three merchant ships fly the Canadian flag on the oceans of the world. Our oil, bauxite, and our general cargoes are all imported in foreign vessels for a fee. Our wheat, coal, aluminum, steel and general manufactured goods are exported in foreign flag fleets, also for a fee, and as previously noted last year that fee came to an estimated $1.5 billion. The current estimated cost of a 14,000 ton dry cargo carrier is $10 million, and I point out to the House that this is an approximate figure depending upon the manner in which that ship is outfitted. If it contains much sophisticated equipment, the cost would be higher but it is roughly $10 million for a 14,000 ton dry cargo carrier. At that cost we could build or buy a fleet of 150 ships from last year's payments to foreign cartels alone, not an inconsequential figure. Yet the agents in Canada for the foreign fleets tell us we would be foolish to build our own fleet. That is their privilege, but I submit we do not have to agree with their viewpoint.
Where in this controversy does our government stand? To be sure, that is a very difficult question to answer. The operative parts of Canada's shipbuilding acts were lifted wholesale from the 1947 legislation. The planners in Ottawa who drafted the 1966 National Transportation Act apparently were unaware, when they slavishly copied the old act, that in 1947 we had a fleet of over 300 ships, while in 1966 we had less than 10. Obviously the planners did not
[Mr. Crouse. 1
know this fact. It is equally obvious that if they did know it they did not care.
As a matter of fact any decision on shipping policy must still be made by the entire cabinet, and everyone familiar with the cabinet and the changes that have been made within it in the past year will quickly realize why no decisions have been made-why it was not until 1975 that the government even moved to set up the otherwise ubiquitous interdepartmental treaty despite years of public protestations.
The former minister of transport did nothing toward building a national flag fleet. He found himself unable or unwilling to overcome the resistance of the foreign lobby which perpetuates the status quo. He followed, if I may say so, the usual Liberal policy-do nothing and maybe everything will turn out all right. I submit that is not good enough at the present time.
In my opinion the world climate is definitely threatening our continued reliance upon foreign fleets. We can no longer assume that the foreign fleets will always be there-always ready to serve-always following the dictates of the dollar. This is not always true. The dollar sometimes takes second place to politics. Take oil, for example. Clearly the dollar is no longer supreme. When some countries wish to affect foreign policy they do so by withholding or diverting oil shipments. We must act to ensure that we will never be immobilized by instabilities in the world shipping community. Only a Canadian owned, Canadian manned and Canadian operated merchant fleet is capable of providing this type of guarantee.
In order to bring this about, in my view there should have been companion legislation introduced with Bill C-61-legislation which would serve to encourage Canadian entrepreneurs to invest in a new Canadian deep sea fleet. At present we have ship construction subsidy regulations whose objective is to assist the shipbuilding industry by subsidizing construction at a level comparable to the tariff protection given to other industries.
All builders of commercial and fishing vessels are eligible for assistance, and a subsidy of 17 per cent is paid on commercial vessels, while a subsidy of 35 per cent is paid on the approved cost of fishing vessels. The seaweed in the propeller of this plan, however, is that the government has not made available sufficient subsidies to cover even the cost for those who would be desirous of building fishing vessels to say nothing about those who may wish to build a ship to expand the Canadian merchant marine.
This House and the Canadian people need an assurance, by example, that the government means business when it plans to expand Canada's merchant fleet. A suitable amount of money must be set aside to cover the existing subsidy legislation. In addition I believe there should be a schedule of concessions to assist shipbuilders and owners in order to re-activate the industry.
I am not proposing an increase in the present subsidy but I am proposing some concessions which should be established, and which would be applicable to ship owners desirous of building new ships in Canada. In view of the large amount of capital required to build a new ship at the present time, the concessions to which I refer should be in
November 26, 1975

the nature of capital loans and interest. For example, the interest on loans should be the prime rate of interest as charged by our chartered banks, less a suitable percentage point over a ten year period.
If a ship is built in Atlantic Canada, for example, the owner should receive a loan at the prime rate less 4 per cent for building in Atlantic Canada, or 3 per cent for building in central Canada. This would stimulate the industry in Atlantic Canada where the present unemployment rate is higher than elsewhere. In addition, if the loan is repaid in less than ten years, or within a five year period, there would be an additional 1 per cent concession on the interest rate applicable to the loan, thereby using the carrot and the stick approach to encourage entrepreneurs to develop a viable shipbuilding industry in Canada.
There would be some cost to the treasury in a program of this type, but a lowering of the unemployment rate from 8 per cent to 4 per cent or less would more than wipe out the cost of the program to the central administration. It would also provide untold employment opportunities ashore and afloat for thousands of presently unemployed Canadians.
This afternoon we heard the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) speak on this bill. He referred to proposed clause Bll-24 (1) and (2) which reads:
(1)	A central office for the filing of documents relating to ships owned by persons qualified to own Canadian ships shall be established in the National Capital Region described in the schedule to the National Capital Act..
(2)	The minister shall provide, within the National Capital Region, a suitable place for the proper functioning of the office of the registrar, together with such furnishings and equipment as are necessary for the performance of the duties allocated to him.
That clause shows better than any words I could use the centralistic spirit of the government. Here we are talking about a maritime code. We are talking about establishing new opportunities for Canadians expanding a maritime fleet. Obviously this type of expansion would have to take part either on the Atlantic coast or the Pacific coast. Certainly if we were to have an office anywhere to deal with this problem it should be a regional office located in Atlantic Canada to serve that area, and I dare say a regional office in central Canada, likely in Montreal, where the bulk of shipping is concentrated, plus another one in the west to serve the Pacific.
Instead of that we read about establishing an office in Ottawa. Of all the things in Ottawa I submit this one is not required. The government should give serious consideration to amending that clause of the bill. I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who first raised the point, and I hope the clause will be deleted or amended to read that the national office will be in the areas affected.
In closing I think it is fitting to place a few of the recommendations of the Darling report on the record. After all, the report was commissioned by the marine transport division of the Department of Transport. No doubt it cost Canadians a considerable amount of money, so I think some of the recommendations should be on the record for consideration when thinking about the requirements of a new marine fleet.
The summary of the contents of the report is quite lengthy so I shall only place a few recommendations on the
Maritime Code
record. In the summary dated October, 1970, Mr. Darling stated:
(1) The negative attitude to international shipping policy in Canada has been due, on the one hand, to unrealistic demands for Canadian flagships having no solid basis in concrete Canadian interests, and on the other hand, to an indifference based on a confidence in the workings of a highly competitive international shipping industry ...
(3)	The varied conditions applying throughout international shipping furnish the context for decisions on Canadian shipping policy. International shipping remains competitive, but its competitive nature is changing. Competition in a free market is diminishing, but competition between large shipping consortia backed in many cases by their states is increasing as it is also direct competition from national fleets that define economic decisions differently. Canada, with its hands-off policy is close to becoming a unique case among the world's main trading nations.
That, I submit, is an honour we can well do without. Paragraph 7 of the report states:
The UNCTAD convention on a code of conduct for liner conferences is in reality a high-level endorsation of completely nationalistic shipping policies. Regardless of whether it ever comes into force it is a clear warning to all nations to protect their own interests with regard to the policies it endorses and which are already being practised by some countries on a scale greater than would be justified by the terms of the convention.
Paragraph 9 reads:
In Canada shipping policy is fragmented between different departments and agencies, each having its own priorities and terms of reference. There exists neither a definition of objectives, a unified administration, an authorization of powers for dealing with the subject matter nor any continuity of purpose or effort. Interventions, where possible at all, require a cumbersome procedure, and are necessarily limited to the vague generalities that are all that can safely be deduced from the equally vague guidelines that are available which for the most part must themselves be thought up.
Paragraph 13 reads as follows:
The principal interest situations that would call for attention include:
(a)	The movement of Canadian resources in the bulk trades, such as ore, coal, etc.
(b)	The role of Canadian ships in the development of the Arctic.
(c)	The examination of Canadian interests with respect to the container consortia that have taken over the greater part of the general cargo trade; this would involve the competitive position of Canadian ports as against American ports.
(d)	The consequences of the bilateral shipping policies of other countries.
(e)	The position of Canadian ports as a result of modern shipping trends.
Finally, paragraph 15 reads:
The basic prerequisites of an effective shipping policy include the following:
(a)	A definition of objectives which will make clear the importance of shipping problems in themselves, rather than to regard them as adjuncts and afterthoughts to other policies.
(b)	A unification or a co-ordination of responsibilities.
(c)	The equipping of the authority with powers commensurate with the stated objectives of that policy.
(d)	A flexible and aggressive administration, able to take initiatives in short term situations and to sustain drives for longer term objectives.
(e)	Apart from whatever steps might be taken in particular interest situations, there should also be a general shipping assistance program available on prescribed terms to any Canadian operator which would permit him to take his own initiative in deep sea shipping but would not involve any government responsibility for maintaining the operation. Such a program should therefore not include direct capital

November 26, 1975
Maritime Code
subsidies beyond the shipbuilding subsidies already available, nor
operating subsidies.
That is exactly what I say, Mr. Speaker. I am not advocating, when asking for an improved and expanded Canadian merchant marine, increased subsidies. I made a concrete suggestion, that we utilize the interest rate structure to encourage entrepreneurs to establish new fleets in this country. Basically, my real purpose for making this proposal is this: I wish to strengthen the security of the state. We must strengthen the security of our nation, and the modest cost to the treasury of this proposal can be justified on that basis. I therefore hope the cabinet will give careful thought to my proposal, indeed, to this whole matter, so that the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine will not be unduly delayed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE A MARITIME CODE FOR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those in politics have long contended that the government is the servant of the people. We are prone to ; lake such statements in elections. We say that we want to serve the people, that the government itself is their servant. The term "civil servant" expresses the same philosophy. It means that those engaged in civil work are the servants of the people.
Bill C-61 contains some exemplary features and is long overdue, but denies everything which has been said about governments being the servants of the people. If the government is to serve the people its services should be as available to most people as readily and as efficiently as possible. As I say, Bill C-61, which is to provide a maritime code of sorts for Canada, contains some redeeming and long overdue features. Yet I am advised that one part deals with the transfer of the west coast shipping registry to Ottawa. Obviously that proposal was designed in the interests of bureaucratic efficiency. It will please those in bureaucratic circles interested in bureaucratic efficiency. It will not please those on the west coast who need the services of the bureau, fishermen, tugboat operators, and other ship owners operating on the west coast. What kind of nonsense is this?
Why is the government to move, almost as far as geographically possible, from the west coast the very service which the people on that coast need? The ship's registry in Vancouver is an active office, and the heavy use made of it shows that it should stay there. Obviously the provision referred to ignores needs on the west coast, and overlooks the efficient and effortless registration of ships in the Vancouver area.
Vancouver is the busiest port in the country and its registry office the largest in Canada, with more than 10,000 ships on file. Some 400 new registrations were added this year. The work is done by a staff of four, headed by the registrar, Stan Baker, and the operation of the office is noted for its smooth efficiency. One can rest assured that if the registration is moved to Ottawa the number of office workers engaged in registering will mushroom upward dramatically; that will happen if the office is moved from Vancouver to the breaucratic catacombs of Ottawa. If you want efficiency, how you can make the operation more efficient by removing it from the area it serves is beyond my comprehension.

The existing operation is efficient, yet Bill C-61 proposes closing the office and transferring it to Ottawa, several thousand miles from west coast salt water. A bureaucratic efficiency expert must have thought of this.
It reminds me of the story of the efficiency expert who checked a certain office. He came to the first person, whose feet were on the desk, and asked, "What are you doing?" The guy said, "Nothing." The expert went to the second desk, and found another man with his feet on the desk. He asked, "What are you doing"? The second man said, "Nothing." The efficiency expert said, "Ah, this is duplication." That about sums up the bureaucratic thinking behind the proposed transfer.
I do not support the proposed transfer as the resulting red tape and bureaucratic entanglement will create immense complications for owners of boats, large and small. Right now, owners who want bills of sale, mortgages, or other papers processed can usually count on obtaining service the same day in the Vancouver registry office. No one can tell me that if the operation is centralized in Ottawa for the sake of bureaucratic efficiency that owners and others will be given the same service, especially in these days of postal strikes when telex and other communications services are clogged with heavy use.

Mr. Speaker, there is a member from Saskatchewan telling us how to operate the Vancouver boat registry. That is typical of Liberal party suggestions.
Further to this, every boat over 30 feet in length in British Columbia waters is on file in the Vancouver office. It is ludicrous to ship those files to Ottawa, far from where their usefulness can be appreciated and, above all, utilized. Surely it would be safe to assume that the existence of any system relies on the premise that it is to be efficient, economical, and utilized. The present registry office in Vancouver satisfies all of these criteria.
In the Vancouver office the closing of a contract is simplified immensely. That is hard to believe in a government office. However, physical delivery of the vessel to the purchaser, payment of purchase money to the vendor, and the guarantee of a clear title as transferred can all be done concurrently. If this system is centralized in Ottawa, we can expect confusion, not simplification; expense, not savings; disfunction, not efficiency.
It is common knowledge that correspondence with Ottawa from either coast is notorious for its inefficiencies. I am not prepared to believe that should the ships' office be moved to Ottawa, west coast vessel owners can expect any change in this pattern regardless of how sincere the bureaucrats might be.
I submit that the bill be given careful and diligent consideration by hon. members. I might add that change for the sake of change more often than not provides a
November 26, 1975

disservice and not a service, as it surely will if this bill is passed in its present form. I invite members of the committee, both of the government and opposition parties, to entertain an amendment that will upgrade the value of this bill. I can guarantee that we can anticipate intervention with this kind of amendment by the Canadian Bar Association. They are certainly concerned with regard to the commercial law section and the maritime section.
I encourage the members of the committee to entertain an amendment that will take into consideration the fact that the government ought to be committed to serve the people in a way that is best and gives the most efficient help to them, not to try to remove the services as far as possible from those who need them the most.
