Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay the passage of this bill. However, I want to call the attention of the House to a matter that was alluded to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) and the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen). I refer to the question of whether it is sensible, having regard to the nature of these registry offices, to compile everything in a central registry.
With the greatest respect to the minister from Saskatchewan and his parliamentary secretary, I think the government is making a mistake in doing that. I understand the necessity for the control of ownership of ships, the matter of derelicts, and a number of other reasons for the argument. However, when you consider the location of the registry offices in terms of service to the public, it does not make sense on one hand to move this kind of office to Ottawa when, on the other hand, the government is talking about distributing various offices of the public service across the country. It does not make sense at all. It seems to work against a policy which was announced or discussed on another occasion.
They are wrong, just as they were wrong in terms of convenience to the operation of a particular department, having regard to its function, by moving the cheque processing unit of the Department of Supply and Services out of the central region to Matane, Quebec. I do not say that that will not benefit Matane. Of course it will. However, having regard to the function and the requirement of what the office is supposed to perform in so far as the public service is concerned, this cheque processing operation move from Ottawa to Quebec is a nonsensical decision, equalled only by the decision set forth in this bill to move a service or operation from the west coast and other places. It means they are going to close a great number of offices and centralize them. I see the parliamentary secretary is nodding his head no. This may be a matter we should consider in committee.
I hope that in committee we will consider the question of decentralization of any office of the public service, not in accordance with economic convenience but in accordance with the function and the requirement of that office. When I hear members such as the hon. member for Comox-Alber-ni or the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock, I cannot help but think that this provision in this bill really requires examination. I hope that we will consider it in committee.
Cancer Fund
There is a difference between decentralization of the public service, which I believe is supposed to be done in accordance with certain principles having regard to the function and need of the offices in various parts of Canada, and dispersal of the public service.
Having regard to the function of the public service, the move to Matane was pure dispersal. The government wanted to put something in Matane. It may have had other overtones as well, having regard to the secret documents I produced, really the core documents with regard to implementation of bilingualism in the public service. But I will not deal with that today. However, the question of decentralization is dealt with in those documents. Those reasons are perhaps not the best in terms of the operation of the public service, just as this move to a central registry in Ottawa from the coast and elsewhere has to be explained in committee. There may well be an explanation. However, at the moment it is on questionable grounds.

speechtext: We are happy to expedite the passage of this bill but I think it is worth a brief explanation from the parliamentary secretary. He surely wants to make one.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: KING GEORGE V CANCER FUND WINDING-UP ACT MEASURE TO WIND UP FUND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity of taking part in this debate, partly because it is the first opportunity I have had to pilot a public bill through the House. I hope it is significant that in doing so I am acting in response to a request made by an august assembly of distinguished Canadians who are presently the trustees of the fund, namely, the Right Hon. Bora Laskin, the Chief Justice of Canada, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau, the Hon. Robert L. Stanfield, the Hon. Marc Lalonde, Dr. W. A. MacLean, Chairman of the Canadian Medical Association Committee on Cancer, the late Dr. J. J. Lussier, representative of the teaching faculty of the French-Canadian Medical College, and Mr. J. W. Westaway, Chairman of the Committee on Medical Scholarships of the Canadian Life Insurance Association. Their request was unanimous.
The purpose of the bill is to authorize the trustees to sell, under the supervision of the deputy minister of finance, as honorary treasurer of the fund, all securities and other assets of the fund and to pay the proceeds of the sale, together with all other moneys held in trust in the fund, to the National Cancer Institute of Canada.
The present book value of the fund, and its approximate market value, is about $62,000. Over its life the fund has disbursed an amount of about half a million dollars. The bill- provides for the termination of the trust forthwith thereafter and further provides that, upon payment and termination, the fund and the trustees of the fund, their heirs, executors and administrators, as well as officers and acting officers of the trust, be released and forever discharged from all obligations arising under the fund.
It will be of some interest to Canadians, I am sure, to know that the King George V Silver Jubilee Cancer Fund for Canada was the first effort of our national crusade to raise funds to promote cancer research in this country. The fund was the inspiration of the Countess of Bessborough, wife of the then Governor General, in 1934, and a public campaign for funds was launched.
In June, 1935, the fund was placed by Her Excellency in the hands of the distinguished predecessors in office of the present trustees.
The fund was to be used "in search of relief from the high mortality rate of cancer in Canada" including, without limitation, research, diagnosis or treatment, education, and the provision of scholarships or training. The fund was tremendously successful in the initial years in raising money for its purposes. By December 31, 1938, the public, the federal and provincial governments, and Canadian insurance companies had contributed a total of nearly half a million dollars. The trustees began to make annual grants to the Canadian Medical Association.
In 1946 the National Cancer Institute of Canada was incorporated to be the recognized agency in Canada con-

cerned with cancer research. It is representative of universities, agencies, and organizations which are concerned with cancer. It acts as the co-ordinating agency in connection with cancer research and sponsors and supports research activities throughout Canada.
As early as 1937 there were indications that the fund should not be the means by which public charitable support of cancer research should be funded. In February, 1937, the then Chief Justice of Canada, the late Sir Lyman Duff, as chairman of the trustees, stated that he intended to refuse to continue as chairman if the fund was to be associated with the collection of additional moneys. He believed that such action was impossible because of his position, being incompatible with his responsibilities as Chief Justice. The situation thus arose that the Canadian Cancer Society was recognized as the public charitable organization through which appeals for funds would be made and the Society, in turn, financed the National Cancer Institute. This development left the fund, in effect, in an inactive role.
Over the years the trustees have made contributions to the National Cancer Institute of Canada so that by January 3, 1974, the fund stood at approximately $65,000. Since 1935 the trustees have endeavoured to use the fund to its greatest advantage to promote cancer research in this country. Nonetheless, the purchasing power of the proceeds of investments of trust moneys now represents a relatively small fraction of that originally anticipated. In the past decade it has become necessary for the fund to liquidate capital assests from time to time in order to release sufficient cash for annual payments to the National Cancer Institute of Canada.
Accordingly, when the trustees met in March of this year, all concerned were of the view that the fund should be wound up and the assets of the fund paid over to the National Cancer Institute of Canada. Since, however, the trust deed provides that the fund is to be continued until the trustees are satisfied that mortality from cancer in Canada has been sufficiently reduced, and since the fund is one of national character and importance, the trustees resolved to make the facts concerning the fund known to parliament with the request that parliament be asked to enact appropriate legislation.
I would like to look upon this event, Mr. Speaker, not so much as marking the end of a gallant effort on the part of all Canadians who have participated in the work of the fund since its inception-for the effort continues apace through others who have followed its lead-but as an acknowledgment of the progress that has been made in this country and throughout the world, including the development of other fund-raising bodies in Canada for cancer research much have largely supplanted the leadership that once undoubtedly belonged to the King George V Silver Jubilee Cancer Fund for Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: KING GEORGE V CANCER FUND WINDING-UP ACT MEASURE TO WIND UP FUND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before commenting on the bill, one which we all wish to see pressed forward quickly, I should like to extend my congratulations and the congratulations of my hon. friends to the parliamentary secretary who has just spoken. He has indicated this is the first bill he has piloted through the House on behalf of his minister. I should like to extend congratulations to him, not only on that fact but on his
November 26, 1975

appointment as well, and wish him every success in his new office.
The parliamentary secretary mentioned the leadership which has been given by distinguished Canadians who have acted as trustees of the fund, and who now feel the time has come to wind it up. I am satisfied that Canadians as distinguished as those who occupied the office of trustees of the fund could do nothing but give us a proper recommendation with respect to the operation of the fund and its place in the fight against cancer. What they have really said is that its funds might be better utilized in another way, basically for research into the ongoing battle to eradicate or bring under control a disease that has brought death to many Canadians, and sickness and sorrow to many families.
In saying that we favour the principle of this bill, we might take this occasion to pay tribute to the men and women of Canada in all parts of the country who have volunteered their work in cancer societies throughout the land. They have contributed hours and hours of their time, walking the streets collecting pledges from those kind enough to give. We ought as well to have emanate from this House an expression of thanks to these people, and to those very generous Canadians who have contributed to this ongoing fight against a dread disease.
There is no fooling about the matter, Madam Speaker; there is still a long way to go, and great dedication on the part of many Canadians for many years will be required. There are a lot of unsung heroes on the road to the eradication of this disease and of other illnesses in society. Some of these people are members and officers of cancer societies, national, provincial and municipal, people in constituencies represented by all members of the House. I would not want this opportunity to pass without saying to them, through you, Madam Speaker, that we are grateful for their work. We hope that as a result of their work we will take some giant steps on the road to the eradication of this killer disease of cancer.
As I said at the outset, Madam Speaker, we are prepared to expedite this matter through the House today, and I close by once again congratulating the parliamentary secretary.

subtopic: KING GEORGE V CANCER FUND WINDING-UP ACT MEASURE TO WIND UP FUND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I believe it is an appropriate act on the part of the government to bring in this bill to wind up the King George V Silver Jubilee Cancer Fund for Canada. I am sure we are all grateful to the parliamentary secretary for putting on the record a brief history of the fund and an indication of the amount of money that has been contributed by it to cancer research.
I think it is also appropriate at this time to pay tribute to the work over the years of the Canadian Cancer Society and of the National Cancer Institute of Canada, set up under the auspices of that society. I believe that the parliamentary secretary is quite correct in drawing attention to the research that has been done and to the progress that has been made, and both he and the previous speaker said what should be said when they pointed to the fact that funds are still needed to enable research to be carried out
Cancer Fund
in order to conquer this dreaded killer, the disease of cancer.
I may be getting out on a limb again, but the introduction of this bill does bring something to mind. When I first saw the title I recalled that in the year 1935, when I was minister of a downtown church in the city of Winnipeg, I preached a sermon on the King George V Silver Jubilee Cancer Fund and took some part in encouraging the members of my congregation to contribute to the fund. Little did I think that 40 years later I would be taking part in a debate to wind up that fund. I also recall a death in my own family that year that prompted a particular interest in the question of cancer, and in saying that I am sure I am expressing the interest of a great many people in this country. We hope that research into this disease will not suffer for want of the necessary funds.
We pay our tribute to those who have worked under the aegis of this fund these many years, and we extend our best wishes for continuing success to the Canadian Cancer Society and to the National Cancer Institute of Canada.

subtopic: KING GEORGE V CANCER FUND WINDING-UP ACT MEASURE TO WIND UP FUND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I would like to associate myself with the words spoken by those who rose before me about the parliamentary secretary who made such a good case of presenting this bill and gave a brief history of the fund dealt with in this bill.
I would like also to point out that it is interesting when a member or a minister asks the House for co-operation in giving quick approval to a bill, that those requests should be made in the sense and the spirit shown earlier. One cannot but respond favourably to that request. I suggest that is the way to work in the House if our country is really to have an efficient administration.
With respect to the bill proper I support it wholeheartedly because the fund being wound up under the bill rendered enormous services to the people of Canada. And since the assets are being transferred to the National Cancer Institute it means that all records and whatever research may have been done will also be transferred to it, and that the institute will continue to work in search of means to fight that terrible disease.
I agree all the more with this bill that I was invited on many occasions to co-operate with the Canadian Cancer Society in my province, and as an hon. member suggested quite properly earlier, when I was a little younger I knocked on doors to ask for donations to the Canadian Cancer Society.
I have not forgotten those moments of service to that cause, and I am still very much willing to do everything I can to help the Canadian Cancer Society in its fight against that disease, all the more so that members of my family have been victims of that dreadful sickness.
I therefore support the bill wholeheartedly and trust that the National Cancer Institute of Canada can achieve even more with the support it is given by this bill, so that we may, in the future, hope to discover even more efficient means of fighting cancer.

November 26, 1975
Feeds Act

It is not a realistic approach to the farmers' problems. One of the misfortunes we as members of parliament have to deal with is the fact that a majority of the

agriculture committee do not understand the implications of the problems farmers must face.
This bill in its initial stages appeared to be an innocuous piece of legislation. After we got into it, however, we found it could create a great many problems for farmers in Canada if a bureaucracy in the department decided to make things difficult. I have great respect for the members of the department and what they are trying to do, but we have no guarantee that the people who now represent the Department of Agriculture will always be there, in the positions they now hold. It might well be that some bureaucrat who wants to throw his weight around sometime in the future could create problems for the farmers.

speechtext:
I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) would be the first to say he is not always going to be the minister, yet he is the minister responsible for sponsoring this bill.
Let me put our objections on the record for the benefit of those on this side of the House and all Canadian farmers, so that at sometime down the road, when problems arise, we can look back and show the Canadian people that we tried to protect their rights.
Since coming to the House of Commons I have tried on a number of occasions to get the government to adopt amendments I felt would be beneficial not only to the people concerned but to the government as well. Apparently the government does not accept this type of philosophy. Members of the government apparently feel it is a sign of weakness to accept amendments from the opposition. If this House of Commons is to work in an adequate manner the government must realize that people outside the cabinet and the committee have a certain amount of background knowledge which can be used to the benefit of the Canadian people. In this regard I am speaking of the Canadian livestock producer.
Let me put some comments on the record made by Dr. Black of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association. I am speaking at this time primarily so that not only the members of the House are conscious of the situation, but in order that I can refer to these comments at a future time, if need be. Dr. Black stated before the committee:
First, let me indicate that neither Dr. Barker nor I is in veterinary practice and we have not been for some years, and that we have no monetary interest in this bill.
Our first concern when we read Bill S-10 was with the definition of a feed. We thought the definition as proposed in Bill S-10 was excessively broad.
Later he stated:
The part of Bill S-10, though, that concerns us most is proposed Section 4, and perhaps I could paraphrase proposed Section 4 in a different way from that in which it is written. It means to us that the bill does not apply to a feed that is manufactured by a livestock producer if it has not incorporated into it any drug or other substance that may adversely affect human health.
That is a big "if", Madam Speaker. Let me state now that we on this side of the House, as well as the farmers and the public, are concerned about the health and well being of the consumer. Let us not put that out of proper perspective. Dr. Black states:
November 26, 1975

Now, we assume that since drugs can be construed by most people to have some influence on human health, we assume then that the inclusion of a drug into a feed by a livestock producer would then bring it under the provisions of the act, and herein lies our concern.
This concern was exemplified recently in a meeting we had with people from the Plant Products Division of the Department of Agriculture when we came away with the understanding that in the future the farmer would only be able to put drugs in the feed in accordance with the medicating ingredient brochures, better known as the MIB's, at present put out by the Department of Agriculture. I think most of us realize that feed manufacturers themselves are limited by the MIB's as to what types of medication they can put in a feed, with the only exception that they can put another drug or a different level of drug or drugs for a different usage in a feed if they do so on the basis of a veterinarians prescription. Now we feel this is excessively limiting if the farmers can only put medication in the feed on the basis of the MIB's. The reason for this is that veterinarians and farmers often consider the feed as a vehicle for the administration of a drug to an animal. The drug has to be approved for oral use, it has to be available for that purpose. Under these circumstances, a veterinarian or a farmer may choose to put a drug in the feed, using the feed as the vehicle, if he has to medicate a large group of animals.
Goodness knows, in this land in which we are living we find that the herds, regardless of whether it is hogs, beef, or flocks of chicken or turkeys, are all becoming larger and it is becoming more difficult to treat them in larger numbers. Certainly it is almost impossible to give them individual treatment. This is why it is of utmost importance that farmers be allowed to treat these animals collectively. Dr. Black went on to say:
He may have to medicate hundreds or even thousands of animals in one treatment, therefore, it is unreasonable to expect him to handle each animal individually and to treat them all orally if this indeed is the route necessary in the case. Therefore, we feel that feed should be kept as the vehicle for the administration of medication to animals.
Just this afternoon we came away from a committee meeting at which we learned that there is a shortage of veterinarians in Canada. The Department of Agriculture is making what I believe to be a noble attempt at training a sufficient number of people to become veterinarians.

speechtext:
That is probably a good solution to some of the problems because I imagine he is a very good veterinarian. I am sure he would be one of the first to realize that there is a shortage of veterinarians, and I am sure he would agree with me also that in a great many cases there is a re-occurrence of disease in herds, while there is a possibility that there may not be a veterinarian available to the farmer to have a drug prescribed for his animals.
I think we must be concerned about limiting the farmer in what he can do because of the fact that there is no veterinarian there to prescribe the medicine. I feel also that we must think about the care and well being of the individual animal. I mentioned this before, and I repeat it, because we are all concerned about it. But-and this is the big but-the farmer can put the medicine through the watering system and thus give it orally, or he can inject it into the animal. I am sure that those who have had experience with this method of treatment realize that there is a far greater danger of residue being left in the animal by injection, either intravenous or intermuscular, but this is
Feeds Act
legal. That is why I feel that this bill is poor legislation which certainly will not protect the consumer and it limits the farmer in the treatment of his herds.
I should like to continue reading what Dr. Black said. It reads:
Now, limiting the farmer or preventing him from doing this does not seem to us to be reasonable because, as I indicated before, the drug has to be approved for use in that class of livestock by the people in the Health Protection Branch. It has to also be available in a form that is suitable for livestock. The withdrawal periods and the dosages must be worked out and approved. So, basically, this drug has to have been approved ahead of time for this type of use in livestock.
Also we feel it is unreasonable to restrict the farmer from mixing it in his feed from another standpoint. The farmer can obtain this drug from an outlet, a feed mill or some other place, and he can administer it to the animals, he can administer it individually or he can inject it perhaps parenterally by intermuscular administration or some other means. Often the route of administration, other than administering it in the feed, will result in a greater likelihood of a residue occurring than if the drug is administered in the feed. On top of that, it is a custom or it is an established tradition in Canadian agriculture that a relatively large portion of medicating farm animals is carried out by the farmer and not directly by the veterinarian. Again we feel that this would tend to limit his scope in this area.
I know, Madam Speaker, that perhaps veterinarians would like to have control over this, and we all know that they receive a fee for their services. This adds to the cost of production. Today we heard the Minister of Agriculture discussing the cost of production as it relates to marketing boards.
The more hindrance we put in the way of agricultural production, the more we will increase the cost to the producer. I think we must look at this realistically and we must approach it intelligently. We must realize that the more restrictions we place on the producer, the more difficulties he will have. Ultimately it will either put him out of business or it will increase his cost of production. Therefore we should be reasonable about this.
One of my great concerns is that we are opening up every farm gate in Canada to a health inspector. There is nothing in the act to suggest that the inspector must have a reasonable assurance that some misdemeanour is taking place in the operation. I take exception to that. I feel there should be some provision in the bill which would require the inspector to submit to the farmer his qualifications and whatever other identification he may have and to tell him what he is doing on the property. We know what happened when we were dealing with the right to privacy by individuals in connection with electronic bugging. Surely while this may not come under the same act, the privacy of the agricultural producer is being sacrificed to a degree. Goodness only knows we are losing our freedom fast enough without enacting legislation which would take more away from us.
I feel that this is poor legislation, and I wish to put that on record and to make it abundantly clear. I am not going to try to change this legislation because I have tried too hard on other occasions; in fact we tried to change this legislation in committee. We realize that perhaps there are misdemeanours which should be investigated, and I have no quarrel with the Minister of Agriculture or the Department of National Health and Welfare for enacting legislation which would provide for inspectors to go on any of

Feeds Act
these properties if they can justify their action and feel that they should investigate, but I do not think the assurance of representatives of the Department of Agriculture is adequate when they say that they do not have enough inspectors to go to all the farms in Canada.
Who knows what is going to happen down the road? We are opening up the gate to every farm in Canada for inspectors to walk through, and they do not have to submit any identification to the farm operator in any way, shape or form.
I think this is bad legislation, and that the government is doing a disservice by bringing it in in this manner. Nevertheless the government has a majority; it pushed this legislation through committee and I presume it will push it through the House of Commons. I am not happy with it, and that is one of the reasons why I am pleased at this time to have an opportunity of expressing my concern in this House of Commons.

Madam Speaker, I should like to make a few brief comments on third reading of Bill S-10. I was and still am a member of the Agriculture Committee, and I was there for discussions on this bill and indeed for some of the evidence which was referred to by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers).
I reject the opening remarks of the hon. member. He said that a majority of the government members on the committee are not experienced or knowledgeable in the field of agriculture generally. That certainly is not borne out by the facts, especially when we examine the membership of that committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN DEFINITIONS AND CONTROL OVER MANUFACTURE, SALE OR IMPORTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN DEFINITIONS AND CONTROL OVER MANUFACTURE, SALE OR IMPORTATION
speechtext:
This bill is not really a major agricultural bill, but it is a very good example of how a committee can work. We called in several groups which wanted to appear before the committee, the veterinary association, the feed dealers' people, and another group of people interested in both animal science and nutrition.
We heard evidence from those people and sat down and discussed that evidence with officials from the Department of Agriculture. We discussed another provision with officials from the Department of Justice, and had a good deal of across the table, non partisan discussion in going through this bill, which is really a small bill with about four clauses in it. At this moment I believe it is coming back into the House with three of those four clauses changed.
As I said, this bill is not a major one, but it is an important and an excellent example of how a good committee can function. In this case the Agriculture Committee did a good job in dealing with this bill. We discussed very thoroughly the amendments and their implications.
Clause 1, dealing with the definition of a feed, was changed and narrowed in its scope, as a result of our discussions and the hearings we held. I believe the final clause dealing with penalties was modified, again as a result of discussion. Another one, which I know the hon. member for Red Deer was concerned about and spoke about, and about which I was personally concerned, was

not changed. However, in my estimation it was explained and spelled out by the officials a good deal more clearly than a casual reading of the bill a layman would have done.
Clause 4 deals with exemptions. Where a farmer or producer manufactures his own feed, under certain conditions he is exempt from the provisions of this bill. I think the hon. member for Red Deer is well aware that the old business of a farmer manufacturing his own feed was a fairly simple matter of putting some grain through a hammer mill or a plate grinder, and perhaps combining a few bags of supplement for a few cattle, a few hogs, or a few chickens. That was, perhaps, 90 per cent the case, but the situation today in the livestock industry is a good deal different. We are certainly now in a different era of livestock production in Canada. There are many very large operations with their own facilities not only for making feed, but for manufacturing and developing the same kind of feed. Indeed, there are larger operations than commercial feed mills which are subject to the provisions of this bill.
I do not quarrel with the objective of bringing some of those operating under the auspices of this bill. Many of these operations are vertically integrated, to the degree that perhaps the poultry or other livestock are slaughtered right on those same premises. I interpret the bill quite differently than does the hon. member for Red Deer. Veterinary prescribed drugs can be added to feeds manufactured or put together on a farmer's own premises. By regulation the bill provides for that exemption. That has been done in the past, and this bill does not change that practice, which has gone on through the years.
The bill expands the definition of what constitutes a feed to meet better today's needs. I certainly would not be supporting this bill if I thought it interfered with the rights of farmers to the extent the hon. member for Red Deer suggested. I would not be supporting it if I thought it was that kind of bill, but indeed I do support it, and I believe it contains a couple of changes which bring the bill up to date, and it is more realistic in terms of feed in agriculture today.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BROADEN DEFINITIONS AND CONTROL OVER MANUFACTURE, SALE OR IMPORTATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset I wish to say that this is a relatively small housekeeping bill. If that had not been so, the government would not have entrusted it to the Senate to introduce. In the main the changes which have been made in this bill have been housekeeping changes. Over the years there have been changes in the feed patterns of agriculture, particularly in vertically integrated operations with automatic feeding programs, where it is absolutely necessary to do the miximg either in concert with the feeding arrangements or at least on the farm rather than in mills, as was previously the case.
During the committee discussions considerable evidence was requested and obtained with regard to drugs which are added to feed. There is a fear on the part of consumers and producers that additions to feed may leave a residue in the end product which may affect the health of the nation. No one suggested that the protection afforded in this bill
November 26, 1975

should be extended only to feed mills. It is agreed that it should also be extended to farm feed mixing mills.
It was generally agreed that there are very few farmers who would do anything on their farms which would be detrimental to the end product. It has been said that drugs have to be added to the production cycle of almost all our agricultural products, and that is so. It is also true that there are instructions in the bill about how the drugs will be administered, but departmental officials have not asked for full control of the mixing which may involve adding some drugs. Our acts are sufficiently tight that those drugs can legitimately be administered by following the directions provided.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) reminds me of the person who says we should eliminate the controls simply because they may be abused. There is not very much wrong with most of the prescriptions issued in this country for people who have difficulty sleeping, or who are nervous or suffer from hypertension, but almost all the suicides are as a result of prescribed drugs. So it is not the drugs that are at fault but the way they are administered. If someone is going to administer them in a dangerous manner it is difficult to protect people from that.
I am concerned that in one part of the bill we have added a number of new things to food that are not actually food at all but work in the feed process and biological function of the animal. I do not think the government has ascertained the long range effect of some of these materials such as nitrogen, enzymes, and some of the other things that provide biological function rather than food value. We have not set up long term testing facilities and I think this is a weakness in our agricultural program. Some of these products have been brought about by changes in protein prices throughout the world, but when they are added as a substitute I think our veterinary services should have a testing program, rather than the producing company, to assess the long range effects of them. In some cases those companies have done the necessary research before the department can put on the label the way a product is to be used.
I believe that if someone comes to my farm with a mixing plant they should be subject to the same restrictions as if I take my produce to the feed mill where the mixing will be done under government supervision. I should be protected when it is done by the operator on my farm. As the Minister of Agriculture said, the operator should at least be able to read the label and know how the machine operates, and I should be assured that the mix is of the proper proportions and done under sanitary conditions.
This bill goes back to the Senate, and of course we would improve on anything they can do. We have done so with a couple of small amendments, but of course the Senate may not agree and the bill may come back to this House. I feel, however, that the department has brought the Feed Grains Act up to today's standards by the introduction of these
Feeds Act
changes. I sincerely hope it will give serious consideration to long term testing as I believe difficulties are developing from new materials being used without enough research being done by the government, independent of the company selling a particular commodity.
I am quite pleased that we were able to make a number of changes in the bill, and I appreciate the efforts of those who appeared before the committee. I think their advice was to the point and enabled the committee to make worth-while changes in the bill.

Madam Speaker, I want to say a few words and to present a very persuasive argument that I am sure all progressive members of the House will agree with-including the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay).
I want to object to the way this bill was brought in, through the Senate. It is a government bill introduced in the Senate, and I think the time has come when we as parliamentarians should be responsible for bills in this House and the other place. Senators are not elected; they are not responsible to anyone; they do not have to face re-election. Many of them are appointed because of political I.O.U.s, and in the Senate they represent their party and lobby for corporations.
In principle I object to any government bill being introduced in the other place. All legislation should be dealt with by the elected representatives of the people and not by those who have no responsibility to meet the people in an election campaign. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) would probably agree. He has been outspoken on this subject and it is a pity he is not here today. It is ironic that one of the bills that goes that route comes under his purview. I think my point is valid not just because I think the other place should be abolished-and I think it should-
